title: Rational approximation bounds and tangent at integer arguments

conventions.limits: n tends to infinity through positive integers

named_hypotheses.D: D(c,alpha,Q): c>0, real alpha>=2, integer Q>=1, and for all integer p,q with q>=Q, |pi-p/q|>=c*q^(-alpha). No reducedness condition.
named_hypotheses.P: For every real alpha>2 there exists integer Q_alpha>=2 such that D(1,alpha,Q_alpha) holds.

records.title: Published all-integer eventual lower bound
assumptions: Use the current published OAI.PiExponent.main as an imported source premise; it has not been reverified here.
records.conclusion: For every real alpha>2, there is an integer Q>=2 such that |pi-p/q| >= q^(-alpha) for every pair of integers p,q with q>=Q.
proof_steps: Source inspection: this is the first conjunct of OAI.PiExponent.main and the type of pi_integer_eventual_lower_bound after expanding IntegerEventualLowerBound.
caveats: Each alpha has its own threshold.
Configured permitted axioms do not show that a comparator run succeeded.

records.title: Nearest odd denominator and tangent pole distance
assumptions: n is an integer with n>=1.
records.conclusion: For k=floor(n/pi), q=2k+1 and delta=|n-pi*q/2|, q is the positive nearest odd integer to 2n/pi; |q-2n/pi|<1; 0<delta<pi/2; q<=A*n with A=1+2/pi; delta=(q/2)|pi-2n/q|. If Q>=1 is an integer and n>=ceil(pi*(Q+1)/2), then q>=Q.
proof_steps: Because n/pi is positive and not integral, k>=0 and 2k<2n/pi<2k+2.
Its odd midpoint q is uniquely nearest and within distance less than one.
Multiplying the distance by pi/2 proves delta<pi/2; delta=0 would make pi rational.
The inequality q>=2n/pi-1 gives the threshold implication; q<=2n/pi+1<=A*n uses n>=1.
Factor q/2>0 to obtain the exact approximation identity.

records.title: Reciprocal bound for cotangent of pole distance
assumptions: For the integer specialization, q and delta are as in nearest_odd_denominator.
proof_steps: Set f(t)=sin(t)-t*cos(t). Then f(0)=0 and f'(t)=t*sin(t)>=0.
Divide t*cos(t)<=sin(t) by t*sin(t)>0.
The odd-pole angle addition formulas give |sin(n)|=cos(delta) and |cos(n)|=sin(delta)>0.
records.parity_restriction: The denominator q must be odd to describe a tangent pole.

records.title: Explicit growth from a fixed Diophantine exponent
assumptions: D(c,alpha,Q): c>0, alpha>=2, integer Q>=1, and |pi-p/q|>=c*q^(-alpha) for all integers p,q with q>=Q.
n is an integer and n>=N=ceil(pi*(Q+1)/2).
proof_steps: The selected q is odd, positive, at least Q and at most A*n.
Apply D to p=2n and this q without reducing the fraction.
The exact distance formula gives delta>=(c/2)*q^(1-alpha)>0.
Taking reciprocals gives |tan(n)|<=2*q^(alpha-1)/c.
Use alpha-1>=0 and q<=A*n.
records.parity_restriction: Only even numerators and positive odd denominators are used.
caveats: No converse for all rational numerators and denominators is asserted.
The same proof works for alpha>=1, but records retain the requested alpha>=2 range.

records.title: Globalize an eventual approximation bound
assumptions: pi is irrational (also follows from D by using multiples of a hypothetical rational representation).
records.conclusion: Define c_star=min({c} union {q^(alpha-1)*dist(q*pi,Z): integers 1<=q<Q}). Then c_star>0 and |pi-p/q|>=c_star*q^(-alpha) for every integer p and integer q>=1. Therefore |tan(n)|<=(2/c_star)*A^(alpha-1)*n^(alpha-1) for all integers n>=1.
proof_steps: Each q*pi is nonintegral, so its distance to Z is positive.
The set in the minimum is finite and nonempty because it includes c.
For 1<=q<Q, use |pi-p/q|=|q*pi-p|/q>=dist(q*pi,Z)/q.
For q>=Q, use the original bound and c_star<=c.
Reuse the direct growth proof; every selected denominator is now covered.
caveats: The numerator set is infinite, but dist(q*pi,Z) supplies its minimum at each fixed denominator.
If Q=1, the added finite set is empty and c_star=c.

records.title: Scaled limits from fixed-exponent growth
records.conclusion: |tan(n)|/n^s -> 0 and tan(n)/n^s -> 0 along n>=1. For n>=N, |tan(n)|/n^s <= C*n^(-beta), beta=s-alpha+1>0.
proof_steps: Divide the fixed-exponent growth bound by positive n^s.
The exponent beta is strictly positive, so n^(-beta) tends to zero.
Apply the squeeze theorem to the absolute and signed sequences.
records.endpoint_status: At s=alpha-1 this comparison only proves boundedness; no limit conclusion is made.

records.title: Absolute convergence by fixed-exponent pointwise comparison
records.conclusion: The series sum_{n>=1}|tan(n)|/n^s converges. For every integer M>=N, sum_{n>M}|tan(n)|/n^s <= C/(s-alpha)*M^(-(s-alpha)). Thus sum tan(n)/n^s converges absolutely.
proof_steps: Set r=s-alpha+1>1. The terms are at most C*n^(-r) for n>=N.
Since x^(-r) decreases, sum_{n>M}n^(-r)<=integral_M^infinity x^(-r)dx=M^(1-r)/(r-1).
All initial terms are finite because integer arguments are not tangent poles.
records.endpoint_status: At s=alpha, the harmonic majorant is inconclusive; no divergence claim follows.

records.title: PiExponent gives epsilon-loss tangent growth
records.conclusion: For all sufficiently large integers n, |tan(n)|<=2*(1+2/pi)^(1+epsilon)*n^(1+epsilon). Thus |tan(n)|=O_epsilon(n^(1+epsilon)).
proof_steps: Choose alpha=2+epsilon and c=1 in the source premise.
Apply diophantine_tangent_growth with its corresponding Q_alpha.
caveats: This does not provide a fixed positive c/q^2 approximation estimate or an O(n) tangent bound.

records.title: PiExponent gives every scaled limit above exponent one
records.conclusion: |tan(n)|/n^s -> 0 and tan(n)/n^s -> 0. Eventually the absolute ratio is at most 2*A^((s+1)/2)*n^(-(s-1)/2).
proof_steps: Choose alpha=(s+3)/2, so 2<alpha<s+1.
Use c=1 and the source threshold.
Apply scaled_tangent_limit and simplify alpha-1=(s+1)/2 and s-alpha+1=(s-1)/2.
records.endpoint_status: No conclusion at s=1 is proved.

records.title: PiExponent gives a sufficient series range above two
records.conclusion: sum_{n>=1}|tan(n)|/n^s converges. For sufficiently large integer M its tail is at most [2*A^(s/2)/(s/2-1)]*M^(-(s/2-1)).
proof_steps: Choose alpha=(s+2)/2, so 2<alpha<s.
Apply tangent_absolute_series_sufficient with c=1.
Simplify alpha-1=s/2 and s-alpha=s/2-1.
records.endpoint_status: No claim about s=2 or the full convergence range.

records.title: Cubic tangent limit
proof_steps: Choose alpha=5/2 and c=1 in the source premise.
Apply the growth theorem and divide by n^3.
The resulting n^(-3/2) bound tends to zero.

records.title: Cubic tangent series converges absolutely
records.conclusion: sum_{n>=1}|tan(n)|/n^3 < infinity. For all integer M>=ceil(pi*(Q_(5/2)+1)/2), the tail sum_{n>M}|tan(n)|/n^3 <= 4*A^(3/2)*M^(-1/2).
proof_steps: Choose alpha=5/2 and c=1 in the source premise.
Use |tan(n)|/n^3<=2*A^(3/2)*n^(-3/2) after the source-dependent onset.
Apply integral comparison, integral_M^infinity x^(-3/2)dx=2*M^(-1/2).
Add finitely many finite initial terms.
caveats: No numerical threshold Q_(5/2) was extracted.
No numerical value of the series was computed.

records.title: Repair the reduced-denominator quantifier
assumptions: All but finitely many reduced rationals a/d with d>=2 satisfy |pi-a/d|>=d^(-alpha).
records.conclusion: There is an integer Q>=1 such that |pi-p/q|>=q^(-alpha) for all integers p,q with q>=Q, including unreduced fractions.
proof_steps: Let E contain all exceptional reduced rationals of denominator at least two plus the integers with |pi-r|<1; this set is finite.
Set eta=min({1} union {|pi-r|: r in E})>0 and choose a positive integer Q>=eta^(-1/alpha).
Reduce p/q to a/d with 1<=d<=q.
If a/d is in E, the error is at least eta>=q^(-alpha).
If d>=2 and a/d is not exceptional, use d^(-alpha)>=q^(-alpha).
If d=1 and a/d is not in E, its error is at least 1>=q^(-alpha).
caveats: Do not assume large unreduced denominators imply large reduced denominators.
Apply separately to each alpha>2 when starting from the usual mu(pi)=2 characterization; no endpoint alpha=2 estimate is obtained.
